#The epitope positions identified per influenza subtype
The positions were identified by 3 papers, all of which inherited the definitions and did not derive them de novo.
H1N1 regions are a ClustalW mapping of H3 onto H1 plus entropy refinement
Influenza B regions are an H3 mapping plus entropy and surface-accessibility additions
If you want to take a look further, the VIC list matches the Yamagata-model table

##H1N1 Site Contents Vary by Strain and Study (Deem & Pan, 2009)
The five H1 sites are Sa, Sb, Ca1, Ca2, and Cb.
These epitopes were mapped out by aligning A/PR/8/1934 (H1) to A/Aichi/2/1968 (H3) using ClustalW.
Structural verification superimposed the PDB model 1HGF (H3) against 1RU7 (H1), with alpha-carbon RMSDs (root mean square deviations) across the five epitopes set at 2.18, 0.63, 1.19, 2.43 and 1.90 Å.
Early antibody mapping on PR/8 assigned 9, 6, 6, 5 and 6 residues to Sa, Sb, Ca1, Ca2 and Cb, which map by homology to H3 epitopes B+D, B, C+D, A+D and E respectively
The remaining 31 sites were added by information entropy. They were added under selective immune pressure on the protein surface, with entropy >0.075, computed from 2,294 full-length human H1 sequences
However, external studies show that the residue counts per epitope differ between the classical PR8 map and pandemic strains.
For instance in a comparison study between 2009 pandemic and eurasian avian-like strains, the sites were of sizes 13, 12, 11, 8, and 5 residues respectively.
Site differences between the two strains were at 4 (Sa), 6 (Sb), 6 (Ca1), 4 (Ca2), and 2 (Cb).
A single H128N substitution in Sa was sufficient to cause a four-fold HI change and measurable antigenic drift


##H3N2 sites (Gupta et al., 2006)
This was the reference strain from which H1 and VIC epitope positions were derived from. 
Strain sequences and the five H3N2 epitope definitions were taken directly from one reference. The dominant epitope was selected as the one with the largest amino-acid change relative to the vaccine strain.
The antigenic distance match measure was calibrated so a perfect matches results in a 47% efficacy
The three papers from which these residues were defined took those residues from external references, specifically identified via crystallography and improved with sequence analysis.
This contrasted with papers that defined epitopes and assembled positional data using monoclonal antibody competition and escape mutant selection instead of a fixed residue roster.
Only epitope regions, and not the entire protein, are significantly involved in immune recognition, so any changes elsewhere track poorly with efficacy


##VIC sites (Pan & Deem, 2016)
Epitopes were mapped to the five H3 regions using PRANK MSA (https://ariloytynoja.github.io/prank-msa/).
PRANK allows for gaps and accounts for evolutionary distances. 
A/California/7/2004 was used as reference and for numbering just like in the H1N1 epitope assembly, any epitope site that aligned with a gap in H1N1 was deleted.
High-entropy sites from human B sequences were then added.


##Why the epitope ranges in config.R seem strange
The papers used did not report using the same method
Gupta et al. and Pan & Deem defined these epitope regions for general use. This was specially used for computing antigenic distance. These regions were deliberately enlarged and mapped onto a model strain, such that they represent binding across a whole repertoire and population instead of a single antibody-antigen contact.
Conversely the classical A-E ranges were structures defined on the H3 model.
We guessed right: the discontinuity was due to those sites being clusters of surface-exposed residues brought together by protein folding, instead of a contiguous peptide.
Overall the fraction of substitutions in the epitope dominating the mutations calculate well for antigenic distance and vaccine efficacy estimations; correlation weakens when the whole hemagglutinin is used
